claims.text: An integrated in situ high-temperature chamber coupling synchrotron XRD with TGA can reliably capture both oxidation kinetics and phase stability of high-temperature alloys.
CrMnFeCoNi is a high-entropy alloy suitable for high-temperature oxidation studies.
The starting CrMnFeCoNi alloy is a single-phase solid solution.
A high-temperature environmental chamber, synchrotron XRD, and TGA or mass monitoring can be integrated for simultaneous oxidation measurements.
Temperatures above 800 degrees Celsius are appropriate for observing significant oxidation and phase transitions in the proposed alloy.
CrMnFeCoNi undergoes high-temperature oxidation in air or an atmospheric environment.
Oxide formation occurs concurrently with phase formation or transformation during high-temperature oxidation.
The oxide scales grow while the alloy substrate undergoes phase transitions.
TGA continuously records mass gain caused by oxidation.
In situ high-temperature XRD tracks time-resolved phase formation and transformation during oxidation.
Combining TGA and in situ XRD permits direct correlation of oxide growth rates with the onset and evolution of phase transformations.
Oxidation may produce parabolic mass-gain curves or shifts in those curves associated with oxide-scale formation.
New or shifting XRD peaks can reveal the emergence or transformation of crystalline phases.
The combined method can determine whether oxide scales act as protective barriers that stabilize specific substrate phases.
Conventional TGA and ex situ XRD assess oxidation kinetics and phase evolution separately and may miss concurrent dynamics under service conditions.
The method is most effective where significant oxidation and phase transitions occur, typically above 800 degrees Celsius.
The method's applicability at lower temperatures or under inert atmospheres is uncertain.
Measurement sensitivity, multiphase evolution, and transient phenomena may impede quantitative correlation of mass changes with specific phase transformations.
Failure to obtain a consistent relationship between diffraction changes and mass-gain changes would falsify the proposed correlation.
Failure to obtain real-time reproducible oxidation or phase data would falsify the claim that the integrated method reliably captures both phenomena.
